title: Comparing
intro: This unit is about comparing: *Ankara İzmir'den daha büyük* (Ankara is bigger than Izmir), *Türkiye'nin en büyük şehri* (Turkey's biggest city), *benim kadar uzun* (as tall as me). It ends with two ways an adjective can do more: doubled for strength (*masmavi*, deep blue) and placed before a verb as an adverb (*iyi konuşuyor*, she speaks well).

blocks.text: Turkish adjectives never change to compare: there is no **-er**. Put *daha* (more) before the adjective: *büyük* (big) → *daha büyük* (bigger). What you compare with goes into the ablative `-DAn` ([A1 unit 7](gp-ablative)): *Ankara İzmir'den daha büyük* (Ankara is bigger than Izmir), literally **Ankara, from Izmir, more big**.

With the ablative in place, *daha* can be left out: *Ankara İzmir'den büyük* means the same. Without anything to compare with, *daha* is needed: *Bu daha ucuz* (This one is cheaper). To stress the difference, add *çok* or *biraz*: *çok daha büyük* (much bigger), *biraz daha ucuz* (a bit cheaper).

head: Turkish
English
rows: The train is faster than the bus.
Istanbul is much more crowded than Ankara.

blocks.text: **Less** is *daha az*: *Bu yol daha az kalabalık* (This road is less crowded). *Daha* also goes with *çok* and *az* after a verb: *Ayşe benden daha çok okuyor* (Ayşe reads more than me), *Bu yıl daha az yağmur yağdı* (It rained less this year).

**Pronouns** take their ablative forms, *benden, senden, ondan, bizden, sizden, onlardan*, and the personal ending goes on the adjective: *Ben senden daha yaşlıyım* (I'm older than you). To ask which of two, put `mI` after each: *Çay mı daha ucuz, kahve mi?* (Which is cheaper, tea or coffee?)

items.en: The train is faster than the bus.

items.tr: Kardeşim benden daha çok kitap okur.
items.seg: Kardeşim ben|den daha çok kitap okur.
items.en: My brother reads more books than me.

items.tr: Bodrum mu daha güzel, Fethiye mi?
items.en: Which is more beautiful, Bodrum or Fethiye?

blocks.text: The ablative goes on what you compare **with**, not on what is bigger: *Ankara İzmir'den büyük* is about Ankara. Swap the endings and you swap the meaning.
*Daha* has other jobs: with a negative it means **yet** ([unit 1](gp-time-past)), and after a number **more, another**: *Daha gelmedi* (She hasn't come yet), *bir çay daha* (one more tea).
English **taller than me** and French plus grand que moi put the comparison after the adjective; Turkish puts it before, in the ablative: *benden daha uzun*.
For **the most**, put *en* before the adjective: *en büyük* (the biggest), *en güzel* (the most beautiful), *en ucuz* (the cheapest). *En* is a separate word and never changes.

**In a group.** To say **the biggest city in Turkey**, Turkish uses the genitive-possessive construction of [A1 unit 10](gp-genitive-possessive): the group in the genitive, the noun with a possessive: *Türkiye'nin en büyük şehri* (Turkey's biggest city), *sınıfın en iyi öğrencisi* (the best student in the class).

**With no noun**, the adjective takes the possessive itself and stands for the thing: *Bu restoran şehrin en iyisi* (This restaurant is the best in the city), *Ailenin en küçüğü benim* (I'm the youngest in the family).
*En* also goes with *çok* and *az* and with adjectives used as adverbs: *En çok çayı severim* (I like tea best), *en az*, *en erken* (at the earliest), *en geç* (at the latest).

items.en: Ali is the best student in the class.
I'm the youngest in the family.
What music do you like best?
Come at five at the latest.

blocks.text: Both ends of the group construction are needed: *Türkiye'nin en büyük şehri*. *Türkiye en büyük şehir* is not Turkish, and *Türkiye'nin en büyük şehir* misses the possessive.
*En küçük* and *en büyük* also mean **youngest** and **eldest** in a family: *en küçük kardeşim* (my youngest brother or sister).

sections.title: Benim kadar, senin gibi: as … as, like

blocks.text: **As … as** is *kadar* after the thing you compare with: *Elif Can kadar uzun* (Elif is as tall as Can). With *değil*, it compares down: *Bu film o film kadar güzel değil* (This film isn't as good as that one).

**Like** is *gibi*: *Elif annesi gibi doktor* (Elif is a doctor like her mother), *Çocuk gibi konuşuyorsun* (You're talking like a child). The verb *benzemek* (to look like, to resemble) takes the dative: *Annene benziyorsun* (You look like your mother).

*Kadar* and *gibi* are postpositions ([unit 9](gp-postp-nominative) groups them). After a noun they need no ending, but *ben, sen, o, biz, siz* and *bu, şu* go into the genitive: *benim kadar*, *senin gibi*, *bunun gibi*. *Onlar* stays bare: *onlar kadar*, *onlar gibi*.

**So, this much, how.** With *bu, o* and *ne* as they are, *kadar* measures: *bu kadar* (this much, so), *o kadar* (that much, so), *ne kadar* (how much; how): *Bu kadar pahalı mı?* (Is it that expensive?), *Ne kadar güzel!* (How beautiful!), *Ne kadar?* (How much is it?). Compare *bunun kadar*, **as … as this one**.

**How much?** Four words set the degree before an adjective: *çok* (very), *oldukça* (quite, fairly), *biraz* (a little, a bit), and *pek* (very), which today you hear mostly with a negative: *pek iyi değil* (not very good).

items.en: My brother is as tall as me.

items.tr: Bu film o film kadar güzel değil.
items.en: This film isn't as good as that one.
I don't have another friend like you.
The film is quite long, but good.

blocks.text: *Ben gibi* and *sen kadar* are wrong: singular pronouns need the genitive, *benim gibi*, *senin kadar*. But plural nouns and *onlar* stay bare: *çocuklar gibi*, *onlar gibi*.
*Gibi* covers both English **like** and **as** (*bir kardeş gibi*, like a brother), as French comme does.

sections.title: Bembeyaz, masmavi: completely white, deep blue

blocks.text: To make some adjectives stronger, Turkish repeats their start, up to the first vowel, and closes it with m, p, r or s: *beyaz* → *bembeyaz* (snow-white, completely white), *mavi* → *masmavi* (deep blue). This is intensive reduplication (*pekiştirme*).
Which consonant comes is a matter of usage: there is a tendency, but no rule you can rely on. Learn these forms as words. There are a few dozen in common use, mostly colours, shapes and states.

These forms already mean **completely**, so they don't take *çok*, *daha* or *en*: *bembeyaz bir ev* (an all-white house), not *çok bembeyaz*. They work as adjectives before a noun and as predicates: *Deniz masmavi* (The sea is deep blue).

items.en: The sea is deep blue, the trees are lush green.

blocks.text: *Sapsarı* also describes a face gone pale with fear or illness. And *kara*, an older word for **black**, lives on in *kapkara* and in names such as *Karadeniz*, the Black Sea.

English adds **-ly** to make an adverb: **slow** → **slowly**. Turkish usually changes nothing: an adjective placed before the verb works as an adverb. *İyi* (good) → *İyi konuşuyor* (She speaks well); *hızlı* (fast) → *Hızlı yürüyor* (He walks fast).
Comparison works the same way: *Ali benden daha hızlı koşar* (Ali runs faster than me), *En iyi Elif yüzer* (Elif swims best). *Çok* strengthens: *çok iyi*, very well.

**Doubled adverbs.** Saying a word twice describes a manner spread over time: *yavaş yavaş* (slowly, little by little), *sessiz sessiz* (quietly), *güzel güzel* (nicely, happily), *tek tek* (one by one). *Sık sık* (often), from [unit 4](a2-u04), is one of them.

items.en: The children are playing happily in the garden.

blocks.text: Some adjectives also have a form with `-CA` (*yavaşça*, gently), which [unit 12](gp-ca) explains. The bare adjective is the everyday choice.
French uses a few adjectives this way too (parler fort, voir clair); Turkish does it with almost all of them.

summary: **Comparative**: what you compare with in the ablative, then (*daha*) + adjective: *Ankara İzmir'den (daha) büyük*. Alone: *Bu daha ucuz*. **Less**: *daha az*.
**Superlative**: *en* + adjective: *en büyük*. In a group: *Türkiye'nin en büyük şehri*; with no noun: *şehrin en iyisi*.
**As … as**: *kadar*; **like**: *gibi*. After singular pronouns and *biz, siz, bu*, the genitive: *benim kadar*, *senin gibi*; *onlar* stays bare.
*Bu kadar, o kadar, ne kadar*: so, that much, how much.
Intensive forms such as *bembeyaz, masmavi, yemyeşil, tertemiz, yepyeni* mean **completely** and take no *çok*.
An adjective before a verb is an adverb: *iyi konuşuyor*, *hızlı koşar*. Doubled: *yavaş yavaş*, slowly.
